value.overview: The Common Tern is a medium-sized, long-tailed seabird found across much of the Northern Hemisphere. It breeds in colonies near marine and freshwater habitats, then migrates south after the breeding season. Adults are mainly pale gray and white, with a black cap, deeply forked tail, and a red bill often tipped with black. The species is an agile flyer that frequently hovers before plunging into water to catch small fish.
value.classification: The Common Tern belongs to the order Charadriiformes and the gull and tern family Laridae. Its scientific name is Sterna hirundo.
value.identification: Adults have a black crown, pale gray upperparts, white underparts, a slender pointed bill, and a deeply forked tail. In breeding plumage, the bill is usually red with a black tip; in nonbreeding plumage, the forehead becomes whiter and the bill is darker. The outer primary feathers can appear darker than the rest of the wing. Juveniles are browner above and show a noticeable dark carpal, or shoulder, bar. It is smaller and shorter-tailed than many large terns.
value.rangeHabitat: The Common Tern breeds across temperate and boreal parts of North America, Europe, and Asia, and winters mainly along tropical and subtropical coasts. It uses ocean shores, bays, estuaries, lagoons, tidal flats, large lakes, rivers, and marshes. In Costa Rica it is a regular migrant and nonbreeding visitor, occurring along both the Pacific and Caribbean coasts, especially in coastal waters, estuaries, beaches, and other open wetlands. It is not known as a regular breeding species there.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, migration is reported mainly from late September through November and again from April through May, while some birds may remain during the northern winter. Individuals passing through or wintering in Costa Rica generally use coastal and estuarine habitats rather than inland areas.
value.breeding: Common Terns usually breed colonially on sandy, stony, or pebbly shores, sparsely vegetated islands, marsh islands, lake margins, and occasionally artificial structures. The nest is a shallow scrape lined with small amounts of vegetation or debris. Both adults defend the nesting area and share incubation and chick-rearing duties. Clutch size is commonly two or three eggs. Chicks are downy and mobile soon after hatching but depend on adults for food until they become independent.
value.dietFeeding: Small fish make up most of the diet, supplemented by aquatic insects, crustaceans, and other small marine or freshwater animals. The tern often searches while flying over water, hovers briefly, and dives headfirst to seize prey near the surface. It may also pick food from the water or capture insects in flight. In Costa Rica, migrants and wintering birds feed in nearshore waters, estuaries, lagoons, and other productive coastal habitats.
value.behavior: The Common Tern is active by day and is often seen singly, in small groups, or in larger flocks during migration. It has buoyant, maneuverable flight and a sharp, rasping call. Adults may defend feeding areas or nest sites aggressively against other birds and predators. Outside the breeding season, individuals rest on beaches, sandbars, pilings, buoys, and other exposed structures. Like many terns, it may travel considerable distances between feeding areas and roosts.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to have a declining trend, although the species remains widespread and numerous. Trends vary among regional populations, with some stable or recovering and others showing substantial declines.
conservation.threats: Important threats include loss or degradation of coastal and freshwater nesting sites, disturbance at colonies, predation by introduced or abundant predators, pollution, reduced fish availability, and climate-related changes affecting breeding habitat and food supplies. Migrants and wintering birds can also be affected by disturbance and degradation of estuaries, beaches, lagoons, and nearshore waters in Costa Rica.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect coastal wetlands, estuaries, beaches, islands, and other shallow-water habitats used by migrating and wintering terns. Keep dogs and people away from roosting or nesting colonies, avoid disturbing large concentrations of birds, support sustainable fisheries, reduce plastic and chemical pollution, and participate in responsible bird monitoring through established conservation programs.
